Commentary.Commentary: We are back for West Indies' reply with the bat. The Indian players have scattered to take their fielding positions. For West Indies, Deandra Dottin and Shemaine Campbelle will open the inning. It will be spin to start for India as Shafali Verma has the new ball in hand. Away we go...
.... THE RUN CHASE ...

Ready for the second inning? As the Windies prepare to embark on their run chase, the question lingers, can they successfully chase down the target, or will the Women in Blues' bowling unit rise to the challenge? The stage is set for a riveting second innings. Stay tuned as the first delivery of the second inning is not far away.

Bhatia and Fulmali steadied the ship - Calm was eventually restored through Yastika Bhatia, who handled the turbulence with composure and clarity, picking out the gaps for boundaries while rotating the strike intelligently to keep the scoreboard moving. Bharti Fulmali initially played a supporting role, but as the partnership grew in confidence, she began to find the boundary with increasing regularity, helping India rebuild with purpose. Just when the innings looked to have steadied, however, a fresh twist arrived. Yastika had to retire hurt, and Afy Fletcher pounced on the opportunity ruthlessly. The 39-year-old claimed two wickets in a single over, then returned to snare another in her final over, finishing with a stunning spell of 4-0-23-4 that threatened to derail India entirely. Through it all, Fulmali stood firm, despite watching wickets fall around her, yet refusing to waver. A brilliant half-century from her ensured India crossed the 175-run mark and gave their bowlers something meaningful to defend.

Flying start for India - India's openers set off with clear aggressive intent, taking the attack to the Windies bowlers from the very first ball. Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma constructed a formidable 59-run partnership off just 32 balls, threatening to set the tone for a commanding total. However, the momentum shifted sharply when Karishma drew first blood for the hosts, and from there, the innings unravelled briefly but dramatically. What had been 59 for no loss quickly became 85 for 3, as West Indies claimed three wickets in successive overs to claw their way back into the contest.

Inning filled with drama - What an inning it was! The pendulum of momentum was swinging from one way to the other throughout the inning, but we can say that the Women in Blue will get the slight edge after the completion of the first inning. India Women have posted 179 runs on the board. However, the way they started the inning, we all thought that the scoreline would cross the 200 mark, but the Windies replied well.

That's excellently done in the end by Jannillea Glasgow. Fullish length, slanting it into the pads. Bharti Fulmali lifts it high towards the long on fence. Glasgow gets right on the edge of the ropes and pouches it well, but recognizes that she's about to go over the ropes. She does well to flick the ball back in and keeps it down to two runs. India Women finish with 179/8 on the board.

Commentary.Commentary: All in readiness for the game to begin. The Sophia Gardens is basking in sunshine as the umpires make their way out to the middle, followed by the players of West Indies Women. For India Women, it will be the usual duo of Shafali Verma and Smriti Mandhana to open the innings. Chinelle Henry will take the new ball herself and will look to make good use of the early bowler-friendly conditions.

The stand-in skipper of India Women - Smriti Mandhana says that they were looking to field first as well, and reckons that they have batted first quite a lot in the past few matches. Smriti adds that they have an XI on paper, but will look to give everyone opportunities. On the conditions, she says it is good to have played under different types of English conditions.

The stand-in captain for West Indies Women - Chinelle Henry adds that the pitch has been under covers for a long time and for that reason, they will be bowling first to get the advantage out of it. On the warm-up fixtures, she says that they will try to experiment in this game and try to make changes as they are focusing on their opening World Cup match which is against England.

Old guard vs the new guard - West Indies Women have been one of those disruptive teams that have managed to break the Aussie-English dominance in the women's game and have won a T20 World Cup as well. However, that was in the previous decade and now, their opponents, India, are showing signs of being that team that can do something similar. Both teams are packed with individual talent, but the Indian side looks more balanced and one would expect them to be the favorites in this contest, not by much, though. Welcome to the Sophia Gardens - Hello, and a warm welcome to one and all. The lead-up to the 2026 ICC Women's T20 World Cup continues with another round of warm-up matches. Two games are scheduled to take place today, starting with an encounter between West Indies Women and India Women. This is the first warm-up fixture for both sides, and they will be looking for a win to ease the nerves heading into the main event.
... MATCH DAY ...

Combustion before competition - The ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 is just a few days away. The trophy is polished, the venues are ready, and 10 teams are putting the finishing touches on their preparations. At Sophia Gardens in Cardiff, the final dress rehearsal for two of the tournament's most compelling contenders is about to unfold. India Women and West Indies Women, separated by four spots in the ICC T20I rankings but united by their hunger for global glory  lock horns in a warm-up fixture that carries more weight than its unofficial status suggests. For India, third in the world and perennial semifinalists, this is about shaking off a disappointing series defeat to England and fine-tuning the final pieces of a puzzle that has remained stubbornly incomplete. For the West Indies, seventh in the rankings and written off by many, it's about proving that their recent momentum is no fluke and that the return of their forgotten stars can reignite a sleeping giant. England hangover - India arrived in England with high hopes. They left the three-match T20I series against the hosts with a 2-1 defeat and a set of unresolved questions. Harmanpreet Kaur admitted after the series loss that the team management is 'pretty much clear' about their preferred playing XI, but her actions suggested otherwise. The batting order has been in a state of flux. Yastika Bhatia, returning from a long injury layoff, has been slotted at No. 3 throughout the England series, showing potential with quick cameos, but pushing Jemimah Rodrigues, who has traditionally excelled in that position down to No. 4. Harmanpreet herself has dropped from her customary No. 4 slot to No. 5. The openers have struggled for consistency, and Richa Ghosh has yet to make a significant impact in the lower middle-order. The warm-up matches, Harmanpreet has indicated, will be used to test a few more combinations and give opportunities to players such as Radha Yadav and Bharti Fulmali. Fulmali's only appearance on the tour came in the opening match and she could be in line for more game time in Cardiff. Pace puzzle - The bowling attack faces its own scrutiny. India's pace unit struggled during the series against South Africa earlier this year, with Arundhati Reddy managing just one wicket in four matches at an average of 123, while Renuka Singh Thakur and Kranti Gaud also found it difficult to maintain consistency. In conditions expected to assist seam movement, discipline will be paramount. On the spin front, Radha Yadav, India's second-highest wicket-taker in Women's T20Is is making a return after nearly a year on the sidelines. Her value extends beyond her bowling as she is widely regarded as one of India's best fielders and has added depth with the bat. The warm-up matches represent her final opportunity to stake a claim before the World Cup campaign begins against Pakistan. Tri-series momentum - If India are trying to rediscover their rhythm, the West Indies have already found theirs. The Caribbean side had back-to-back dominant wins to start their tri-series campaign in Dublin. They then suffered a narrow one‑run loss (DLS method) to Ireland, but rain in their final match against Pakistan worked in their favour, allowing them to lift the tri‑series trophy on net run rate. Old stars return - More significant than the results, however, is the personnel. The West Indies have given a chance to their forgotten stars, Deandra Dottin and Stafanie Taylor and both have been recalled for the World Cup squad. Dottin, once the most destructive batter in women's T20 cricket, remains unstoppable when she gets going. Taylor, a former captain and one of the game's most accomplished all-rounders, brings experience and composure to a middle order that has often lacked both. Alongside them, captain Hayley Matthews remains the best player in West Indies cricket, capable of changing a game with both bat and ball. Matthews smashed 82 off just 44 balls in the opening match of the tri‑series, setting the tone for the entire campaign. Depth on display - The depth of talent within the squad has been highlighted by their bowling performances in the tri-series. The 30 wickets taken against Ireland and Pakistan were split among nine different bowlers.  Vice-captain Chinelle Henry delivered an excellent all-round performance (33 runs and 2/13) against Pakistan, earning her Player of the Match honours. Beyond Henry, the spin attack looks particularly potent - Afy Fletcher brings years of experience, Ashmini Munisar has impressed with her left-arm variety, and Karishma Ramharack offers control in the middle overs. Among the pacers, young Jahzara Claxton has shown she can be a handful with her raw pace. Form (Last 5 completed WT20Is, recent first) - IND-W - LLWLW | WI-W - LWWLL. What to expect? This is a warm-up match, and while the result won't be remembered once the World Cup begins, the performances certainly will be. For India, it is about regaining confidence after the England series defeat and settling on a stable batting order, while the West Indies aim to show that their recent tri-series success was no fluke and that their returning stars can deliver on the big stage. India come in with a stronger ranking, deeper squad, and a better historical record, but the West Indies bring momentum, belief, and a full-strength unit for the first time in a while. In Cardiff, on a pitch that could offer something for everyone, the side that controls the middle overs and executes better under pressure will take away more than just a warm-up win.
